messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi, a 52-year-old South Asian man, has been struggling with the aftermath of an event that occurred several months ago. As a maid working at a busy suburban home, Ravi was mopping the floor when he accidentally knocked over a cleaning supply cabinet. The resulting spill led to another worker slipping and sustaining a serious injury. Since then, Ravi's memories have taken on a snapshot quality, with each moment of the accident replaying as vivid pictures in his mind. These snapshots often come unbidden; the sound of a mop swishing across tile or the sight of a cabinet door opening can instantly transport him back to that fateful day. When these memories surface, Ravi experiences intense feelings of rage, directed inward at himself for what he perceives as an inexcusable mistake. Ravi's self-blame has been pervasive since the accident. He is convinced that his actions directly caused the injury and feels a deep sense of violation against his own values. His work ethic had always been impeccable, but this incident has left him feeling that nothing in his life holds meaning anymore. The guilt he carries is overwhelming, and it has colored every aspect of his daily routine. At work, Ravi becomes particularly agitated whenever he hears the clinking sound of cleaning supplies or sees a mop bucket placed near a cabinet. These triggers instantly remind him of the accident and fuel his feelings of self-blame. He has started to avoid certain areas of the house where these items are often found, which has led to conflicts with his supervisors who expect all tasks to be completed promptly. Ravi's personal life has also been affected. Since getting divorced last year, he had hoped to find some semblance of peace and meaning in his work. However, the constant reminders of the accident have made this nearly impossible. He often finds himself staring blankly at the floor tiles or cabinets, lost in thought about how differently things could have gone. The memory of the event continues to reinforce Ravi’s negative appraisals. Each time he relives the snapshots, his sense of self-worth diminishes further, and he becomes more convinced that nothing he does can compensate for what happened. This cycle has left him feeling profoundly isolated and hopeless about the future. Ravi finally decided to seek help after a particularly intense episode at work where he nearly broke down in front of his colleagues. He is most afraid of being seen as a liability, but secretly hopes therapy might help him find some sense of purpose again. His primary fear is that no matter how hard he tries, the memory will continue to haunt him and erode any chance of finding meaning or peace.
